title: Reduced intellectual development in children with prenatal lead exposure.
ehr_evidence: The subjects belonged to a cohort of children born in Mexico City at the National Institute of Perinatology between 1987 and 1992, followed until 2002.
summary: In a prospective cohort of children born in Mexico City (1987-1992) and followed to 2002, higher maternal third-trimester blood lead was associated with lower child full-scale IQ at ages 6-10 years.
key_findings: Higher natural-log third-trimester (28-36 week) maternal blood lead was significantly associated with lower child FSIQ at 6-10 years (β = –3.90; 95% CI –6.45 to –1.36), controlling for other lead and covariates.
Blood lead at week 28 of pregnancy was the only prenatal lead measure significantly predicting lower FSIQ (β = –4.13; 95% CI –6.45 to –1.81; p = 0.0006).
The BPb-IQ dose-response relationship was log-linear, not linear-linear (J-test t = 2.15, p = 0.02).

In the VIQ model, higher 28-36 week BPb was associated with lower verbal IQ (β = –3.15, p = 0.007); in the PIQ model, 28-36 week BPb was inversely associated with performance IQ (β = –4.37, p = 0.004).
No significant association between contemporaneous 6-10 year BPb and FSIQ after adjustment for other prenatal and postnatal lead and covariates.
captured_features: Blood lead (BPb) at prenatal weeks 12-20 and 28-36, and postnatal ages 1-10 years
population: Children born at the National Institute of Perinatology, Mexico City (1987-1992), followed to 2002; 175 children tested after 5 years and 150 with complete covariate data, with IQ assessed at ages 6-10 years.
limitations: Substantial loss to follow-up (from 321 to 175 to 150 with complete data), reducing power and increasing instability of coefficients.
Small sample size limiting detection of subtle effects.
Repeated use of the same IQ test could produce test-learning effects.
Outdated (superseded) Spanish WISC-R and WAIS versions used for IQ measurement.
